title: What each prince saw
hook: Duryodhana and Arjuna look at the same field and see different things
carry: moha clouds the eye; the gita clears it
tomorrow: so what does Duryodhana actually say to his teacher?

segments.voice: Yesterday, reading the Gita's first chapter: svajana, one's own people, and a line that widens the family to the whole earth. This week ran from aham, I, to that wide circle.

The Gita's second verse turns from the blind king to his son. Duryodhana, the prince on the other side, looks out at the Pandava army drawn up for battle, and his first move isn't a speech. It's a look. The verse opens with one word: drishtva. Having seen. Then he walks to his old teacher and starts talking fast. A few dozen verses later, Arjuna looks out at the very same field, and the same word comes back. But he sees something else.
screen: `DURYODHANA LOOKS.` → `DRISHTVA: HAVING SEEN.` → `ARJUNA LOOKS AT THE SAME FIELD.`

segments.voice: The verse: drishtva tu pandavanikam vyudham duryodhanas tada, acharyam upasangamya raja vachanam abravit. Drishtva, having seen; the -tva ending means having done it. Upasangamya, having gone up to his teacher. Abravit, he spoke, waiting at the very end. Duryodhana sees an army, and an army is all he sees: rivals, numbers, a war to win. Now Arjuna, later in the chapter: drishtvemam svajanam krishna yuyutsum samupasthitam. Having seen these, my own people, Krishna, standing here wanting to fight, my limbs give way. Listen: drishtva, svajana, yuyutsu, three words from this very week in one breath. Same field, same verb, and Arjuna sees family. Here's the teaching, and it runs the length of the Gita. Arjuna's seeing is tender, but it's also clouded: grief and attachment, mine and theirs, have bent it, and Krishna's whole teaching sets out to clear it. The tradition's word for that cloud is moha, delusion born of attachment. At the very end, in chapter eighteen, Arjuna says: nashto mohah, smritir labdha. My delusion is gone; I've remembered. The Gita begins with two men seeing and ends with one seeing clearly. And this week's words are that path in small: aham and vayam, I and we; atman, the self that isn't killed; maya, hard to cross; the I-maker that claims the deed; yuyutsu and jijnasa; svajana, and the earth as family.
screen: `DRISHTVA: HAVING SEEN.` · `DURYODHANA SEES AN ARMY.` · `ARJUNA SEES HIS OWN PEOPLE.` · `MOHA: THE CLOUD ON THE SEEING.` · then, large: `THE WEEK, IN SMALL WORDS.`

segments.voice: Hindus have a word for holy seeing: darshan, going to the temple or the home shrine to see God and be seen. Try a small darshan now. If you have an image of a deity, or a photo of someone you love, rest your eyes on it; if you don't pray, choose one person's face in your mind. Breathe, and just look, slowly, the way the verse puts seeing first. Then try seeing them as one of your own, and let the seeing come clear before anything is said.
Reading the Gita's first chapter: today, drishtva, having seen, the word that opens Duryodhana's look and Arjuna's. And moha, the cloud on the seeing, which the Gita ends by clearing.
Your line: moha clouds the eye; the Gita clears it. Two princes, one field, and a week of small words.

fork.setup: at the Gita's very end, Arjuna says nashto mohah, my delusion is gone. what has the whole conversation done?
